entities.name: Herman I, Count of Salm
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Herman I, Count of Salm, born circa 1035, emerged from the Luxembourgish nobility to become a pivotal, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, figure in the Investiture Controversy, serving as elected German anti-king from 1081 until his death on October 4, 1088. His election by the Saxon and Swabian magnates represented a direct challenge to Emperor Henry IV's authority, deepening the schism within the Holy Roman Empire and extending a conflict that would define the era. As the progenitor of the House of Salm, his dynastic legacy endured, yet his political career was inextricably linked to the struggle between papal and imperial power.

Following the death of Rudolf of Rheinfelden, the first anti-king, Herman was elected by the opposition princes at Ochsenfurt on August 6, 1081. Despite the initial support of Pope Gregory VII and the Saxon nobility, his reign was characterized by limited territorial control and constant military engagement against Henry IV. He initially received backing from Welf I, Duke of Bavaria, and the Swabian forces, but his influence largely remained confined to Saxony. A significant setback occurred in 1086 when he suffered a defeat at the Battle of Bleichfeld against Henry IV, further diminishing his already precarious position. His inability to establish broad recognition across the Empire underscored the deep divisions and the enduring strength of the imperial party.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Herman I's seven-year anti-kingship significantly prolonged the Investiture Controversy, forcing Emperor Henry IV to contend with internal rebellion and contributing to the long-term decentralization of imperial power.
